title: A celestial arch illuminates the desert
caption: The arch of the Milky Way over the control building, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Seen from the control building of ESO's Paranal Observatory, home of the Very Large Telescope (VLT), the Milky Way forms a great arch over the Chilean night, with the Magellanic Clouds to its left. The bright area toward the top left of the arc is the galactic center, 27 000 light-years away.

Our galaxy measures between 100 000 and 200 000 light-years across and holds billions of stars besides the Sun. The Sun takes almost 250 million years to circle the galactic center once, and it has completed approximately 20 such orbits since it formed.

Those two fuzzy patches, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, are among our galaxy's neighbors, orbiting at about 160 000 and 200 000 light-years respectively. Both dwarf galaxies are irregular in shape, possibly because of gravitational tugs between the two and from the Milky Way itself.
scale: ESO gives the Milky Way's diameter as between 100 000 and 200 000 light-years, with the galactic center 27 000 light-years away.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/M. Zamani. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds may look brighter here than they would to someone outside the building.

explore: Paranal's telescopes can be thought of as its eyes, and the control building as its brain. Besides offices, it houses the control room, where every telescope and instrument is operated and aimed at its targets, and where a first check of the incoming data takes place.
alt: The Milky Way arching across a night sky over an observatory building, with two fuzzy patches, the Magellanic Clouds, on the left.
